findings: SQLite-backed Durable Object storage is transactional and strongly consistent and private to the object.
transactionSync executes a synchronous callback in a transaction and rolls it back if the callback throws.
transaction executes storage operations in one transaction that commits or aborts; SQLite direct storage operations participate in the transaction.
No current primary-source statement was found that transaction callbacks are automatically replayed; D0019 does not depend on callback retry behavior.
blockConcurrencyWhile blocks other events and is commonly used for constructor initialization/schema work.
If its callback throws, the object is terminated/reset; it has a 30-second timeout.
Regular SQLite storage operations are synchronous and do not yield the event loop; D0019 therefore does not use long external I/O under blockConcurrencyWhile.
A Durable Object instance can be evicted/reconstructed; in-memory state is not a durable authority and constructor initialization runs again on a new instance.
Global uniqueness is enforced on new events and storage access, but a long-running event that never touches storage can become non-current during replacement/network partition/software update.
D0019 therefore requires authoritative mutations to touch durable storage and does not treat in-memory singleton identity as semantic proof.
Uncaught object or infrastructure exceptions propagate to callers.
retryable errors are suggested for retry only when the application request is idempotent/safely repeatable; overloaded errors should not be retried.
A stub should be recreated after an exception.
An exception is not evidence that the semantic mutation did not commit; D0019 reconciles by durable request receipt.
Calls on the same stub have E-order semantics, but a thrown exception poisons in-flight/future calls on that stub; this is not an exactly-once request guarantee.
Alarm handlers are at-least-once and are retried after uncaught failure with exponential backoff for up to six retries.
D0019 does not use alarms as command-admission authority.

Name-derived Durable Object routing supplies a stable object identity within the selected namespace/jurisdiction; D0019 uses canonical Case ID routing but does not infer semantic authority from routing identity alone.
SQLite storage is bounded per object; current paid-plan limit is 10 GB.
Maximum string/BLOB/table-row size is 2 MB, SQL statement length 100 KB, and maximum bound parameters per query 100.
D0019 production storage must normalize/chunk authoritative data rather than store an unbounded Case snapshot in a single row/blob.
Current declarative exports lifecycle supports created/deleted/renamed/transferred classes and replaces the legacy migrations lifecycle for Workers that adopt it.
A Worker cannot return to legacy migrations after deploying exports.
New namespaces use SQLite and a provisioned namespace storage backend is immutable in place.
These provider deployment constraints do not authorize a tdev semantic Case authority migration.

A.name: CaseDO hosts/adapts the existing D0010/CaseEngine semantic authority
A.reason: It preserves the existing semantic state machine and changes the physical transactional adapter/placement, not the meaning. Provider SQLite transactions plus object routing are sufficient primitives when all authoritative reads/writes and receipts are persisted in one object transaction and no external side effect occurs inside it.

B.name: explicit migration to ad-hoc CaseDO-native durable state
B.reason: Any semantic rewrite is unnecessary and risks observable drift. A source-to-destination copy without an independently durable old-writer fence was executably falsified: both stores accepted different commands from the same revision and diverged. Existing local Cases therefore remain with their current authority until a separate migration/cutover Design owns the placement generation and exclusive writer barrier.

C.name: different single-owner equivalent instead of CaseDO
C.reason: No repository or provider evidence falsified the bounded SQLite-backed CaseDO host/adaptor model. An equivalent remains architecturally legal only if later evidence falsifies CaseDO production qualification; it is not needed to close the Design question.

migrationCutover.currentD0019Decision: no migration of an existing locally authoritative Case in the initial D0019 implementation
migrationCutover.newCasePlacement: after production qualification, a new Case may be born directly in its CaseDO and has no local semantic co-owner
migrationCutover.existingCasePlacement: existing local Cases remain writable only by their existing owner and must not be exposed as writable CaseDO copies
migrationCutover.futureMigrationPrerequisite: a separate accepted migration/cutover Design must define a durable placement generation, exact old-writer fence, source quiescence barrier, destination activation, read ownership, in-flight command treatment, duplicate receipt transfer, response-loss handling, restart/retry proof, rollback boundary, and completion evidence
migrationCutover.rollback: before any Case is born in CaseDO, code/config rollback may remove the unused adapter; after a CaseDO Case exists, rollback may only deploy a schema/semantic-compatible CaseDO implementation and must not route that Case back to local authority
migrationCutover.downgrade: no silent storage-backend downgrade, namespace reprovision, or semantic-owner downgrade; incompatible schema/backend lifecycle changes require a separately accepted migration/rollback plan
